articles.title: 32 departures who could define the 2026 NFL season
articles.summary: Can the Ravens' o-line improve without Tyler Linderbaum? Will Mike McCarthy just be a lesser version of Mike Tomlin?
articles.body:
The NFL is a league defined by parity. A hard salary cap means all 32 franchises have to prioritize their spending. It also means saying goodbye to key contributors when their contract demands outstrip their team's budget restrictions.

Every team has at least one notable hole to fill in 2026, whether that's from aging veterans, stars who priced themselves out of a locker room or coaching staffs that didn't work out. Some of them will be filled effectively, keeping playoff teams on the road to the Super Bowl or helping set the foundation for a revival. Others will be mortal wounds that chase these rosters to the top of the 2027 NFL Draft.

Let's look at each team and see if we can't single out the losses that loomed largest this offseason — and whether they'll play a role in their 2026.

The 40-year-old didn't fit with Arizona's rebuild, but his veteran leadership could be missed on a roster with multiple rising young talents in the trenches. Both Walter Nolen and Darius Robinson are recent first round picks with room to grow. Campbell's presence could have helped a coaching staff short on established names.

Swapping out Elijah Wilkinson for Jawaan Taylor at right tackle — blind side for Atlanta's lefty QBs — is effectively sending an undercooked meal back to the kitchen in exchange for a burnt one. But losing Elliss, Ruke Orhorhoro and Leonard Floyd takes away three of the team's most effective pass rushers (in terms of pressure rate) leading into a season where James Pearce will serve an eight-game suspension after being charged with domestic abuse.

Jalon Walker's season-ending preseason injury doesn't help either. 2025 saw an often toothless pass rush rise up to second in the NFL with 57 sacks. Replicating that will be difficult.

The Ravens lost a handful of key blockers, including the occasionally frustrating Daniel Faalele and run-blocking specialist tight end Charlie Kolar. None had a greater impact on the offense than Linderbaum, whom the Ravens hoped to re-sign this spring only for the Las Vegas Raiders to jump in and completely reset the center market by offering him $27 million annually. While his blocking in both phases of the game was an obvious strength, his ability to diagnose defenses pre-snap could have a quieter, but similarly important, effect on how Jesse Minter's first offense as head coach looks.

Bills leadership decided good was the enemy of great and fired McDermott, who won nearly two-thirds of his regular season games as the team's head coach over the previous nine seasons (98-50). In his place is promoted offensive coordinator Joe Brady, whose screen-heavy attack doesn't exactly inspire confidence. Brady's been blessed with some of the best quarterbacks in the world in his coaching career (Joe Burrow at LSU, Josh Allen in Buffalo) but has to prove he shaped their careers and not the other way around.

The long-tenured head coach worked wonders with the defense, crafting a top-five unit four of the last seven years. But that group backslid the last two seasons and the rise of the New England Patriots spurred a move that could either unlock a new level of play for the Bills or a whole lot of regret.

Carolina did strong work reinforcing its roster leading into the season that will ultimately decide whether the Bryce Young/Dave Canales era is worth sustaining. One potential weakness, however, lurks at running back. Dowdle remained found money in 2025, average 0.6 rush yards over expected (RYOE) per carry in a 1,000 yard campaign. Chuba Hubbard shared time with him and averaged -0.3 RYOE per touch.

Jonathon Brooks was a 2024 second round pick, but has nine below-average NFL handoffs to his credit in two seasons thanks to injury. Could Trevor Etienne, once healthy and back on the active roster, be the unlikely hero of this group?

The Chicago secondary is replacing three players who played at least 97 percent of its snaps as well as C.J. Gardner-Johnson. But while Robinson isn't a big loss on his own, he represents a missed opportunity to improve a position of need. The Bears' 31.6 percent pressure rate ranked 27th in the NFL last season . The team's 35 sacks were a bottom-10 number.

Robinson wouldn't have changed that, but the fact remains there isn't a new arrival who can be counted on to patch up a potentially fatal flaw. Chicago will rely on Dayo Odeyingbo and Grady Jarrett to have bigger impacts in their second seasons with the team and Austin Booker and Shemar Turner to make leaps in their third and second NFL seasons, respectively.

Cincinnati Bengals: EDGE Trey Hendrickson

In 2024, Hendrickson's last dominant season, the Bengals had a 31.8 percent pressure rate and a 22 percent blitz rate — both 22nd-highest in the league . In 2025, where Hendrickson played only seven games due to injury and played well below his standard following an offseason contract debate, the team's pressure rate rose to 32.6 percent (still 22nd) while the blitz rate fell to 19.4 percent (31st). This, paired with significant veteran additions up front, provides hope Cincinnati can not only keep things together in a post-Hendrickson pass rush, but even emerge as an above-average unit.

The additions of Dexter Lawrence and Boye Mafe bring veteran experience up front. Three recent first or second round picks — Myles Murphy, Shemar Stewart and Cashius Howell — will work to revive the defense around them.

Jared Verse is a very good player who has the unenviable task of replacing one of the best sack artists in NFL history. Verse will now inherit Garrett's double-teams, as no full-time pass rusher on the roster last fall recorded a pressure rate above 10.4 percent.

It's still a key departure if the guy leaving makes you better on his way out. Eberflus was dealt a tough hand when Micah Parsons was traded before the 2025 season, but he took a bad Mike Zimmer defense (31st in points allowed) and somehow made it worse.

His inability to adjust from a rigid cover-two scheme left Dallas fitting square pegs into round holes for an undermanned unit. He couldn't work out how to mitigate a lack of pressure. He failed to divert responsibility from an ineffective linebacker corps. Many of those problems remain — why, again, did the team trade Osa Odighizuwa? — but now Christian Parker is tasked with building that group into something more than the sum of its parts.

Denver was arguably one injury away from a Super Bowl appearance and paying a quarterback on a rookie contract, so it largely kept the band together for 2026. Swapping out Joe Lombardi for Davis Webb at offensive coordinator could create issues, but Sean Payton's history suggests a smooth transition.

Instead, let's look at the underappreciated Franklin-Myers. The defensive lineman has been a consistent pressure generator from his end spot, and while his pressure rate dipped to a career-low 11 percent last season — still good! — his 7.5 sacks were third-most on the team. Can recent third round picks Tyler Onyedim and Sai'vion Jones fill the void he leaves?

Anzalone was a sigil of Detroit's rise under head coach Dan Campbell. A part-time starter in New Orleans, he arrived in 2021 and immediately stepped up his game. The off-ball linebacker provided the high leverage tackling expected (albeit with some inconsistency), but shined as a high motor pass deterrent who allowed a passer rating under 86 in four of his five seasons with Campbell. While newly extended Jack Campbell can fill some of the leadership void he leaves behind, an iffy cornerback rotation raises further questions about the Lions' coverage.

There have been several departures on the offensive side of the ball, from key wideouts (Romeo Doubs, Dontayvion Wicks) to key tailback depth (Emanuel Wilson). Walker didn't make the free agent splash expected after signing a one-year, $4 million deal with the Carolina Panthers, but Green Bay could still regret letting him walk.

His place at left tackle will be filled by 2024 first round pick Jordan Morgan, who was soundly underwhelming playing primarily as a guard in 2025. The Packers are optimistic enough about his future to let Walker, uh, walk… but the depth behind Walker and right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele is limited.

Houston didn't lose much after a third-straight playoff appearance. It's made a heavy wager on yet another offensive line revamp, however. Former high value draft picks Howard and Juice Scruggs are out — the former was inconsistent and the latter generally failed to make a positive impact.

In their place are established veterans like Braden Smith and Wyatt Teller, two players on the wrong side of 30 who each missed at least four games in both 2024 and 2025. It's a change that had to be made, but one that could collapse inward at a key moment.

Indianapolis Colts: WR Michael Pittman Jr.

Was Pittman the spoon that stirred the drink in Indy? He was the team's second-most valuable receiver last fall, bouncing back from a subpar 2024 to provide a reliable mid-range presence who found space for easy gains. 2025 saw him lead all Colts non-running backs in average separation (3.0 yards) and catch rate (72 percent ). He was second only to Tyler Warren in terms of targets, which will leave Daniel Jones in search of a new safety valve when he returns from a torn Achilles.

Pittman was costly compared to his production, but his presence helped everyone else in the offense operate smoothly in space. Will his absence make life difficult enough to erase the gains we saw from Jones, Warren and Alec Pierce last fall? Can an aging Keenan Allen fill the role he left behind?

Losing Travis Etienne isn't ideal, but the Jaguars thrived despite a slightly below average run game last season (and Bhayshul Tuten is fun. Good? Maybe! Fun? Absolutely). Instead, let's look at a secondary that could be a heavyweight at corner (a full-time Travis Hunter and a better-than-you-think Montaric Brown) but has questions to answer at safety.

Wingard wasn't remarkable, but he was a reliable veteran presence who emerged as a starter over seven seasons as a pro and was a useful presence against the pass (a -4.9 percent catch rate over expected as the closest defender last fall). Eric Murray is 32 years old and facing an age cliff. Antonio Johnson was awesome in 2025, but had struggled a season before.

If Johnson's five-interception breakthrough is sustainable, Wingard will be reduced to a guy remembered across Duval County. If he backslides, the Jags could be liable to allow a handful of devastating big plays this winter. A big debut from rookie third rounder Jalen Huskey or a rise from 2025 third rounder Caleb Ransaw would help restock the depth in center field as well.

Kansas City Chiefs: 60 percent of the starting secondary

Trent McDuffie, Bryan Cook and Jaylen Watson all departed this offseason, leaving a roughly league-average passing defense behind for greener pastures. That's a lot of production to backfill with minimal space, so Kansas City opted to trade up and make Mansoor Delane the sixth overall pick of this spring's draft (Jadon Canady followed in round four) while signing Alohi Gilman and L'Jarius Sneed to relatively inexpensive deals (Kader Kohou and Kaiir Elam were there as well but failed to make the 53-man roster). There's a bit of a duct tape feel to this group that will be tasked with shutting down the AFC's top quarterbacks. Squint hard enough and it makes sense.

Carroll's final(?) act in the NFL was the equivalent of watching Randy Moss in a Tennessee Titans jersey. In his place comes Klint Kubiak, fresh off making Sam Darnold a Super Bowl winning quarterback. His playcalling before 2025 isn't exactly inspiring; a mediocre 2021 Vikings team and a bad 2024 Saints one.

He's been risk averse (with Kirk Cousins in '21) and a risk taker (Darnold's 18 interceptions in '25), but generally willing to adjust to the strengths his roster provides. In 2026, that means bringing Fernando Mendoza along slowly and relying on Brock Bowers and Ashton Jeanty long enough for proper reinforcements to arrive in 2027.

A swap between Harbaugh brothers helped unlock Oweh's potential. After a 10-sack 2024, he'd been shut out through the first five games of the regular season with the Baltimore Ravens. He joined the Chargers after Week 5 and had 7.5 sacks his final 12 games. His 17.3 percent pressure rate was tops among the team's full-time pass rushers and higher than contemporaries like Myles Garrett, Aidan Hutchinson or Danielle Hunter.

He's a Commander now, leaving the pass rush to Tuli Tuipulotu and a 35-year-old Khalil Mack. Both those guys are great (18.5 sacks, 92 pressures between them), but the depth behind them will rely heavily on first round rookie Akheem Mesidor turning his many years of college experience into Week 1 production.

Durant was the Rams' top corner last fall, allowing only a 70.9 passer rating across 68 targets when split wide. He's a Dallas Cowboy now, which would be a much bigger concern had general manager Les Snead not raided the Chiefs' secondary for its top two corners this offseason.

Jaylen Watson and Trent McDuffie will bring an immediate upgrade to the secondary as a whole, though Durant's familiarity with defensive coordinator Chris Shula could make his shoes difficult to fill. Still, 2026 was an all-in moment for Los Angeles. There aren't many holes in this roster that haven't been patched.

Miami Dolphins: WRs Jaylen Waddle and Tyreek Hill

Malik Willis' top wideouts for 2026 are some combination of Malik Washington, Jalen Tolbert, Chris Bell and Caleb Douglas. Greg Dulcich might be a late bloomer at tight end — a position that typically requires a long NFL runway — but 2025 was his first season with a positive EPA when targeted. De'Von Achane has been healthy the past two seasons and was fourth in the NFL in rush yards over expected last fall, but he's about to see the most stacked boxes of his life as opponents dare Miami to throw downfield.

Minnesota Vikings: EDGE Jonathan Greenard

Greenard's sack number slipped from 12 to three last season, but his underlying numbers suggest he remains a dynamic force from the edge. His pressure rate rose to 15.4 percent — two points higher than it was in 2024 — and he was on pace for 58 pressures and 17 quarterback hits over a 17-game season.

Those aren't necessarily double-digit sack indicators, but show he was still a valued member of one of the NFL's most chaotic forces. Despite those three sacks, he was Minnesota's most effective pass rusher last fall. The hope is Dallas Turner is ready for his superstar turn after a solid 2025, but he may have to shoulder the bulk of the load if a 31-year-old Andrew Van Ginkel begins to show signs of an age related decline (he was still good in 2025, despite fewer sacks).

New England Patriots: EDGE K'Lavon Chaisson

Jaylinn Hawkins' departure in the secondary was patched with an aging Kevin Byard and an ascending Craig Woodson. Backfilling Chaisson's pass rushing presence will be more difficult; he led all regular edge rushers with a 14.2 percent pressure rate . His 52 pressures and 7.5 sacks were both second on the team.

Dre'Mont Jones was signed to replace him. With 30 extra pounds he'll bring additional bulk against the run and can play on the line, but he's a less effective player on passing downs. Rookie second round pick Gabe Jacas has dealt with injury and an unusual contract holdout before joining the team midway through the preseason. It's entirely possible a pass rush that struggled to turn pressure into sacks last season backslides this fall.

The Saints swapped out an inside linebacker in his late 30s making his return to the team that drafted him with… a less heralded inside linebacker in his early 30s, making his return to the team that drafted him. This is not a knock on Kaden Elliss, who emerged as one of the league's best blitzing off-ball players after leaving New Orleans in 2023. Elliss's return brings a player who has posted a missed tackle rate under seven percent in each of the last four seasons and who has recorded at least 100 pass rush reps every year in that span (he topped out at 21.5 percent pressure rates in 2023 and 2024, showcasing how effective he can be even if opponents are expecting him).

Coincidentally, Davis returned to the New York Jets after eight seasons (and five All-Pro nods) in Louisiana. The veteran isn't the force he once was, but he remained a steady tackler who was a force meeting tailbacks at the line of scrimmage. His deficiencies in coverage late in his career won't see much of a backfill with Elliss in town, which could leave New Orleans vulnerable in the middle of the field — and that's before taking in the veteran leadership he brought to the locker room.

The Giants need open targets to keep Jaxson Dart from scrambling face first into the concussion protocol. Robinson picked up the slack following Malik Nabers' injury last season, but now he's a Tennessee Titan. This would be a pothole and not a collapsed bridge on New York's road back to prosperity if not for concerning reports about Nabers' rehab. If the third-year wideout can't play effectively, Dart's top wideouts will be some combination of Darius Slayton, third round rookie Malachi Fields and a very washed combination of Darnell Mooney and Odell Beckham Jr. (it pains me to put Mooney here, but good god, his 2024 ).

Robinson expanded his route tree last fall to be more than just a short-range target. His true value came after securing the ball. His 419 yards after catch were 11th-most in the NFL — exactly the kind of production that boosts a young quarterback. The Giants may have correct not to pay big on one year of notable production, but if Nabers can't go this wideout depth chart starts to look a bit… depressing.

New York Jets: Coordinators Tanner Engstrand and Steve Wilks

Most of New York's most notable personnel departures happened before last year's trade deadline. Understanding this left head coach Aaron Glenn in an awful spot with an already bad team, the Jets brought him back for a second year but fired the support staff around him.

Frank Reich won a Super Bowl calling plays for Nick Foles in 2017 and dealt with the wrath of David Tepper in his 11-game stint in charge of the Carolina Panthers in 2023. His biggest challenge, however may be coaxing another revival from Geno Smith — 2025's 35th best starting quarterback in a field of 37.

That lift is only slightly lighter for defensive coordinator Brian Duker. The 37-year-old is younger than his starting middle linebacker (Demario Davis is about six months older) and has never served as a full-on coordinator before. He inherits a defense loaded with a strange blend of veteran talent and young prospects, many of whom haven't played together before 2026.

More high profile players left in bigger deals — A.J. Brown and Jaelan Phillips — but Blankenship's departure shines a light on a potential weakness in the Philadelphia defense. Despite an electric young cornerback trio, the Eagles are set to start some combination of a) an August 2025 cut-down day casualty of the New England Patriots (Marcus Epps) b) a 2025 second round pick who struggled against the pass as a free safety before getting injured (Andrew Mukuba) c) a slot corner who played only 24 snaps aligned at safety last season (Michael Carter II) and d) a seventh-round rookie relegated to the practice squad after cutdown day (Cole Wisniewski). Blankenship had flaws, but he was a stable option in what looks like a volatile rotation for 2026.

Tomlin ruled the sideline at the former Heinz Field for 19 years. He recorded a losing record in zero of them. His ability to keep Pittsburgh in playoff contention but, after 2016, out of Super Bowl contention eventually limited the franchise's rebuild options. So, in his place comes… a head coach who wins a ton of regular season games and falls apart in the postseason.

Mike McCarthy's return to the sidelines leaves him exactly as far removed from his last Super Bowl appearance as Tomlin. He's 6-8 since hoisting the Vince Lombardi trophy and his last postseason game saw him get thoroughly ruined by the Packers, becoming the only team in NFL history to lose to a No. 7 seed in the process. This is all to say things have changed for the Steelers, but may look remarkably similar once the season begins.

Winters had his flaws, but played capably alongside Fred Warner before the perennial All-Pro was lost to injury. Getting to play next to one of the league's best defenders is a pretty big caveat, but the undersized off-ball linebacker put in work to ensure teams couldn't simply pick on him when Warner was there. He allowed only 4.8 yards per target in coverage while lined up at linebacker, though his limitations were more apparent when Warner wasn't there to cover for him.

Warner gets a new/old running mate with the return of Dre Greenlaw, who was limited to seven starts with the Denver Broncos last year but was credited for only a single missed tackle in 44 opportunities . If Greenlaw can get back to his 2023 form at age 29, this is an upgrade. If not, Winters could be missed (though dealing him for Osa Odighizuwa was the right decision).

Attrition hit the Seahawks less harshly than most reigning Super Bowl champions thanks to a massive investment in the team's foundation. Kenneth Walker was backfilled by Jadarian Price and the presence of Zach Charbonnet. Riq Woolen's departure may hurt, but he was inconsistent and saw his playing time hit a career low in 2025. Boye Mafe will be missed, but Derick Hall was similarly productive in fewer snaps and produced a higher pressure rate.

The player Mike Macdonald may miss most is Bryant. The rangy safety wasn't infallible, but he was a key deterrent downfield — see his four interceptions without a touchdown allowed while lined up deep, as well as an -8.1 percent catch rate over expected in coverage . Ty Okada, who allowed 75 percent of his targets to be caught as closest defender when lined up at free safety, has big shoes to fill.

David finally retired this offseason, though he's mentioned returning to play alongside Rueben Bain . There's no easy replacement for a 14-year veteran who made himself fundamental to Tampa Bay's identity. Ultimately, however, David was a step slower in his mid-30s, leading to declining coverage skills and rising missed tackle rates.

The concern now is that the players signed to replace him have similar issues. Christian Rozeboom struggled in coverage and missed nearly one out of every eight tackling opportunities last season. Alex Anzalone can replace some of David's leadership and is coming off another solid season, but his 32nd birthday approaches and an age-related decline could follow. The pressure will be on rookie second round pick Josiah Trotter to make an immediate impact and carry David's banner forward in Florida.

Tennessee Titans: OLs Lloyd Cushenberry and Kevin Zeitler

Cam Ward's 37.2 percent pressure rate was a bottom 10 figure among starters, though it was exacerbated by his tendency to hold the ball (and a lack of receivers who could consistently get open). That led to a league-high 55 sacks last fall. Tennessee's 2.5 yards before contact per carry was roughly league average. Cushenberry's play fell from his previous highs, but he's a high-level pass blocker at his best. Zeitler remained one of the most reliable guards in the NFL.

But Tennessee let Cushenberry leave for an inexpensive deal with the Buffalo Bills and Zeitler is staring down retirement. That leaves new additions Austin Schlottman and rookie Day 3 draft pick Fernando Carmona (who is better than his draft position suggests) as replacements. Early returns have been positive, but we'll have to see if they can team with Peter Skoronski to be absolute road graders up front.

The Commanders couldn't have known Las Vegas would blast through the contract curve and give Tyler Linderbaum $27 million annually. It still doesn't explain why they released an above average center making a reasonable $10 million per year. Replacement Nick Allegretti didn't exactly inspire confidence in limited action last season — and even though Biadasz suffered a preseason injury that will keep him off the field this season, his absence will still be felt.

articles.title: Jaguars receive just a few votes as analysts predict winner of AFC South
articles.summary: A number of analysts recently predicted the winner of the AFC South, with the Jaguars receiving just a few votes.
articles.body:
Over at NFL.com, 19 analysts submitted their votes for who they believe will win the AFC South this season. The Jacksonville Jaguars received just three of those votes.

Leading the way were the Houston Texans , who received 15 votes. The Indianapolis Colts received one vote, and the Tennessee Titans didn't receive any.

"We know the Texans have an elite defense, but their offseason moves to beef up the running game should pay off by taking pressure off C.J. Stroud and allowing the offense to operate more effectively," wrote Lance Zierlein.

The Jaguars secured the AFC South title last season, fending off the Texans by winning their final eight games of the regular season.

During that stretch of games, the Jaguars boasted one of the most productive offenses in football, led by Trevor Lawrence and the passing game. The defense was one of the stingiest, while also continuing to be one of the best at generating takeaways.

As good as last season ended up being for the 13-4 Jaguars, a reason for continued optimism heading into 2026 is the value of continuity. Rather than implementing new schemes on both sides of the ball, Jacksonville was able to spend this offseason building upon the strong foundations that have been established.

Liam Coen discussed early on in training camp how he uses the lack of national recognition as fuel for his team. Perhaps this article from NFL.com will be the latest example of that.

articles.body: Aaron Rodgers already knows what he wants once his NFL career comes to an end. The Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback has confirmed that the 2026 season will be his last, but retirement will not simply mean walking away from football. Rodgers now has a much more personal goal in mind, one that involves his wife Brittani and the family life he hopes to build after spending more than two decades in the league.For Rodgers, this next phase has been on his mind for some time. In a conversation with Washington Post columnist Salena Zito in August 2026, he opened up about his plans beyond football and gave a rare glimpse into the life he wants with Brittani once his playing days are over. Aaron Rodgers has fatherhood in mind after his Steelers farewellRodgers made his plans clear during his conversation with Zito, which The Washington Post published on September 2, 2026. Discussing what he wants from life after football, the Steelers quarterback said, “My next chapter in my life is fatherhood.” He then made one point clear: “We are not expecting yet, but I cannot wait to be a father.”The comments add a personal touch to what will already be a significant season for Rodgers. On May 20, 2026, he confirmed that the upcoming campaign would be his final NFL season, ending a career that began with the Green Bay Packers in 2005. Rodgers later joined the Steelers for the 2025 season and returned to Pittsburgh for one final run in 2026.Now, his attention has started to move beyond the game. Fatherhood gives Rodgers a goal that has nothing to do with statistics, playoff runs or another contract. More importantly, he has made it clear that he wants that future with Brittani.Rodgers has kept his marriage extremely private, and Brittani has largely stayed away from the spotlight. That has made every comment he shares about their relationship stand out. He has previously explained that his wife does not want the public attention that often follows NFL players and their partners, preferring to keep their personal life away from social media and cameras. Brittani has become an important part of Aaron Rodgers’ life after footballAlthough Rodgers rarely discusses his marriage in detail, his recent comments show just how much Brittani has influenced his life away from the field. He has credited her with helping him reopen communication with his family, something he discussed while reflecting on the changes in his personal life.During an interview with NFL Network in August 2026, Rodgers explained that getting married and having conversations with his wife helped him become open to rebuilding those family relationships. He said, “A big part of it was getting married and having those conversations with my wife that allowed me to kind of open up of the possibility of coming together.”He also added, “Having her by my side during this process has been really special.”That helps explain why Rodgers sees life after football differently now. His final season with the Steelers gives him one last chance to compete, but he already knows where he wants to go afterward.Rodgers has also suggested that he plans to stay away from the spotlight once his NFL career ends. He has no need to keep chasing another football opportunity, and his latest comments suggest that home life will take priority instead.For now, though, there is still one season left. Rodgers will try to make his final Steelers campaign count before turning his attention toward the life he has been waiting to start.And if his plans stay on course, his biggest achievement after football may have nothing to do with the NFL at all.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. She once described her hunger for online attention in blunt terms, saying:“I will do anything for a viral video on this app.”That ambition helps explain why Netflix is such a significant step. TikTok gave Earle control over what audiences saw. A reality series changes that equation. Her family, relationships and personal conflicts become part of the entertainment, creating both opportunity and risk.Tom Brady adds an interesting layer to the sports connection surrounding Earle’s rise. articles.title: Bears' Updated Salary Cap After Reportedly Restructuring 3 Contracts Ahead of 2026 NFL Season
articles.summary: Chicago Bears general manager Ryan Poles could be clearing space for a roster move ahead of next Sunday's season opener at the Carolina Panthers.
articles.body:
Chicago Bears general manager Ryan Poles could be clearing space for a roster move ahead of next Sunday's season opener at the Carolina Panthers.

The Bears created about $17 million in 2026 salary cap space by restructuring three contracts, ESPN's Field Yates reported Friday.

The contracts impacted belonged to guard Joe Thuney, defensive end Dayo Odeyingbo and linebacker T.J. Edwards, according to Yates.

Chicken equity? This may be the wildest jersey number trade yet

The move could potentially create about $4.5 million in cap space for the Bears. Over the Cap projected they were about $12.5 million over the 2026 salary cap prior to the moves.

All three players are currently signed through the 2027 season. Thuney was carrying a $21.5 million cap hit distributed between a $16 million base salary, $5 million signing bonus and $500,000 workout bonus prior to the restructuring, according to Over the Cap .

Over the Cap reported Odeyingbo carried a cap hit of $20.5 million ($15.5 million base salary, $4.5 million signing bonus, $500,000 workout bonus).

Edwards carried a $10.8 million cap hit ($8.25 million base salary, $2.3 million signing bonus, $250,000 workout bonus), per Over the Cap .

The trio's combined cap hit will now be reduced from $52.8 million to about $35.8 million, according to Yates.

The news comes after ESPN's Dan Graziano reported the Bears are "still looking for a strong edge presence opposite Montez Sweat."

Graziano reported Poles "has been an active and aggressive trader in his time with the team, and he'll turn over every rock he can looking for an impact player up front."

That report led to speculation tying the Bears to Arizona Cardinals edge rusher Josh Sweat, although Graziano reported earlier this week the Cardinals have told other teams they aren't interested in trading Sweat.

The salary cap moves also come as the Bears brace for upcoming contract negotiations with quarterback Caleb Williams, who will be eligible for an extension next offseason.

Keeping salary cap space open for the 2028 season could be key as Williams looks to raise the price of his extension with a strong upcoming campaign.

articles.title: “It was strictly professional”: Dianna Russini’s Mike Vrabel review reveals what The Athletic found in 903 stories and 204 podcast episodes
articles.summary: NFL News: The much-awaited moment is here. Dianna Russini’s review involving Mike Vrabel is out. It was conducted by The Athletic’s editorial director for stand.
articles.body: The much-awaited moment is here. Dianna Russini’s review involving Mike Vrabel is out. It was conducted by The Athletic’s editorial director for standards and quality, Mike Semel. But before we get to that, here’s a little preview of why the review was conducted in the first place.Dianna Russini worked as The Athletic’s senior NFL insider from August 2023. She appeared on the website and app, as well as in audio and video content.On April 7, 2026, she reached out to The Athletic and The New York Times Company executives to inform them that a Page Six article would suggest a romantic relationship between her and Mike Vrabel, the New England Patriots head coach.She said the story would be based on photos of them together taken at a Sedona, Arizona, resort. The photos would come out with the story.She acknowledged a “close relationship with Vrabel,” but emphasized that “it was strictly professional.” She also said there would be no more photos of them together because she “had never done anything inappropriate.”Dianna Russini and Mike Vrabel internal review finds conflict of interest but mixed resultsThe Athletic publicly supported Dianna Russini when it began an internal investigation into the reporter-coach allegations involving Mike Vrabel.During the investigation, Russini submitted her resignation. The Athletic released her from her contract on April 14, 2026.The Athletic ended its investigation into her personal conduct then but continued its investigation into her journalism. Why? “Because nothing is more important to The Athletic than its credibility and reader trust,” Mike Semel wrote.What The Athletic internal review examinedThe review examined:903 stories and 77 videos published on The Athletic website and app that had Dianna Russini’s byline, co-byline, contributor line, or a reporting mention.204 Scoop City podcast episodes produced by The Athletic and co-hosted by her.25 off-platform appearances or interviews.14 The Athletic staffers who worked closely with her.75 stories involving Mike Vrabel or his teams [the Tennessee Titans and New England Patriots] for comparison with other publications.The conflict of interest was the biggest problem in Dianna Russini’s case.Russini’s relationship with Vrabel was a clear conflict of interest under The Athletic’s standards, irrespective of whether the relationship was romantic. It was a breach and should have been revealed.“To maintain the highest form of authority, we should avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest and reveal those sources or affiliations that may put into question our ability to be credible,” Mike Semel wrote.The review found limited coverage of Mike VrabelOut of the 903 stories Dianna Russini wrote, 5 percent were about Mike Vrabel or his team - 46 stories. In 32 months of employment, she wrote only three stories that had unusual depth on Vrabel. Of those three, only one carried her name.Out of 77 videos, only three were about Vrabel. They were light-hearted: what annoys him, 50 questions for his 50th birthday, and a third video that posed him as heroic after he broke up a fight during the Patriots and Commanders training camp.Out of 204 podcasts, Russini hardly mentioned Vrabel’s name.The Athletic staffers said Russini knew several coaches, former coaches, coordinators, front-office executives, and owners. She also shared her sources with staffers. And the staffers did not suspect she was closer to Vrabel than anyone else.Accuracy, bias and some awkward and uncomfortable praise for Mike VrabelThe review found no inaccuracies in Russini’s stories about Vrabel or his teams, except for the “What I’m hearing on Mike Vrabel, the Steelers, the Chiefs and more in NFL Week 12” article.Russini wrote in that article:“Angry Tennessee Titans fans can stop hoping owner Amy Adams Strunk fires Vrabel. It’s not happening. Based on multiple conversations with high-ranking Titans officials, the franchise strongly and collectively believes it has the right coach for long-term success.”The article followed widespread media questions about Vrabel’s job security, and less than two months later, he was fired.“No other media had come out as strongly about Vrabel’s job security,” Mike Semel wrote.Most columns Russini wrote about Vrabel or the Patriots were news-focused and transactional. There was no clear link to ascertain that she used her platform to promote him or his teams during her time with The Athletic.Instead, there were places where she “glowingly” wrote about him. In hindsight, they were “awkward” and even “uncomfortable.”Before Vrabel’s first face-off as New England Patriots coach against his former team, the Tennessee Titans, Russini described Vrabel as someone who had taken “something that used to be a mess” and reshaped it “into a competent operation.”She also wrote that Patriots owner Robert Kraft “has his quarterback but just needed the right man to lead his organization after Bill Belichick’s flameout and the Jerod Mayo disaster.”“Vrabel was once Tennessee Tough. Now he’s returning as New England’s hero. Even though he may be downplaying it, Patriots players want to make a statement for their coach to show they have his back,” she wrote.Dianna Russini further elaborated on why the Titans owner fired Mike Vrabel“Adams Strunk hired [Brian] Callahan because many in the building believed he was everything [Mike] Vrabel wasn’t - quieter, softer, more collaborative.She’d grown tired of Vrabel’s act, even if she respected his coaching chops. Vrabel is loud, direct, and unapologetically himself. He’s not for everyone. But he never lost his locker room.Under Vrabel, the Titans reached an AFC Championship Game, consistently overachieved and, most importantly, had an identity.And if there’s one thing Tennessee should’ve learned from his tenure, it’s this: Nobody ever questioned who the Titans were when Mike Vrabel was their leader. Since they fired him, that’s all anyone wants to know. Who are the Titans now?”While Russini’s prose sounded gushing about Vrabel, Mike Semel noted that other publications, including FOX Sports and ESPN, were also “fawning in writing about Vrabel’s return.”On the Scoop City podcast, Vrabel was described as a “leader of men” and a “CEO-style coach.” Russini pitched him for the Chicago Bears job in a December 2024 episode.In July 2024, Russini and the co-host steered the conversation toward how good a coach Vrabel was.In January 2025, when the Titans GM was fired, she said the team probably regretted firing Vrabel. In August 2025, the last part of an episode featured a lighter rapid-fire Q&A about Vrabel’s pet peeves.The Athletic review’s final decision on Dianna RussiniThe review reached two key conclusions:Russini did not disclose to her editors a clear conflict of interest.The Athletic’s standards on such issues are robust, but they are subject to employee honor, candor, and transparency.Mike Semel further suggested tighter standards for The Athletic to ensure something of this nature does not happen again:New employees should spend 30 minutes with the Standards Editor during the onboarding process to ensure accountability and an understanding of expectations.The Athletic should clarify its conflict-of-interest guidelines.Editors must ask their reporters who their anonymous sources are, even for insider transactional news.Reporters must answer their editors honestly and immediately.The recurring use of the same source should spark additional reporter-editor conversations about the nature of the source relationship.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: New Baker Mayfield Rumors Detail QB's Frustration with Bucs Contract Talks Ahead of 2026 NFL Season
articles.summary: Quarterback Baker Mayfield reportedly wasn't thrilled with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers' unwillingness to compensate him similarly to comparable quarterbacks during recent contract talks.
articles.body:
Quarterback Baker Mayfield reportedly wasn't thrilled with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers' unwillingness to compensate him similarly to comparable quarterbacks during recent contract talks.

According to ESPN's Jeremy Fowler (h/t ESPN's Jenna Laine ), Mayfield used Jordan Love of the Green Bay Packers, Trevor Lawrence of the Jacksonville Jaguars and Brock Purdy of the San Francisco 49ers as comps for the type of deal he was looking for.

While Mayfield was not looking to "reset the market," the Bucs reportedly offered him a two-year deal worth just north of $100 million. An average annual value of $50 million would place Mayfield just 13th among quarterbacks.

Love and Lawrence have an AAV of $55 million, while Purdy is at $53 million, and Mayfield reportedly wasn't happy with the length and guaranteed money attached to the offer the Bucs made him in relation to those contracts.

Per Laine, a league source anticipates that the $50 million AAV benchmark for quarterbacks will soon balloon to $60 million because of Lamar Jackson, C.J. Stroud, Caleb Williams, Drake Maye, Bo Nix and Jayden Daniels all being in line for new contracts soon.

That suggests that if Mayfield had signed a $50 million AAV deal, he would have quickly been pushed down the pecking order in terms of QB compensation.

Mayfield was outspoken about his frustrations regarding his contract talks with the Bucs during training camp, telling reporters , "That's really the disappointing part—to feel undervalued after thinking you've earned it."

The 31-year-old veteran, who has already said he will not negotiate a new deal during the season, added, "If you've waited this long to take care of your franchise quarterback, that's too bad because it's only going to get worse from here. I'm going to have a really big year."

Mayfield is set to enter his fourth season with the Bucs and the final year of his current contract.

Over his first three campaigns in Tampa, Mayfield went 27-24, led the Buccaneers to a pair of playoff appearances and earned two Pro Bowl selections.

He also collectively completed 66.3 percent of his passes for 12,237 yards, 95 touchdowns and 37 interceptions.

The 2018 No. 1 overall draft pick has resurrected his career with the Bucs after failed runs as a member of the Cleveland Browns and Carolina Panthers, and he would undoubtedly be a desirable quarterback option in free agency.

Of course, the Bucs could always place the franchise tag on him to prevent that from happening next offseason, but if Mayfield does enjoy another strong year in 2026, the price to sign him to a longer-term deal will continue to rise.

articles.title: Fantasy Football 2026 Sleeper WRs to Target in Updated Flex Rankings
articles.summary: Boom-or-bust outcomes are somewhat unavoidable when it comes to a sleeper receiver in fantasy football.
articles.body:
Boom-or-bust outcomes are somewhat unavoidable when it comes to a sleeper receiver in fantasy football.

If they had a higher baseline, then they probably wouldn't qualify as sleepers. The same holds true if they didn't offer rather significant growth potential.

So, a bit of risk-taking is a must here, but that's true any time it comes to chasing potential. NFL teams don't stake a Super Bowl run around a solid and safe group of players, and fantasy managers would be similarly denied of their championship dreams if they took the same approach.

The risk factor comes from the fact these are largely dart throws, but the good news is those tosses shouldn't cost you a lot. To up your odds of striking a Bull's-eye, we'll spotlight two of our top sleeper targets at receiver after updating our flex rankings.

With the amount of sleeper hype surrounding Downs, you might think the helium would've floated him out of sleeper range by now. That just hasn't happened. His draft cost has climbed a tad (real-time ADP: 101.6 , per FantasyPros), but nowhere near the point of significantly impacting your profit potential.

He has a history of making the most of his opportunities. Across his first three NFL seasons, 198 of his 293 targets were caught. The one inconsistency in his profile has been volume. It felt like a big target spike might be coming last season, and then he wound up seeing a career-low 88 targets in 16 contests.

Maybe we'll all be duped again, but it sure feels like all arrows are pointing toward that spike still coming—just a season later than expected. Michael Pittman Jr. is gone, Alec Pierce only recently returned to full-practice duties after offseason ankle surgery and Keenan Allen, a 34-year-old, only joined this team last month.

Downs has proved a potent option in the slot, but his downfield responsibilities could trend way up. And if they do, he could be remembered as one of the biggest fantasy steals of the season.

While the fantasy community is collectively (and understandably) fawning over 49ers rookie De'Zhaun Stribling, there hasn't been nearly enough digital ink spilled over Samuel's prospects upon his return to San Francisco.

The same availability concerns surrounding other aging or unavailable playmakers propping up Stribling should apply to Samuel, too. In fact, the veteran might be even better positioned to seize upon these chances, since he can slot both at receiver, where Ricky Pearsall is out, Christian Kirk is on injured reserve and Mike Evans is having trouble staying on the field, and at running back, where 30-year-old Christian McCaffrey is coming off of a 450-touch season.

The 49ers lost their yards-after-catch magic last season, which Samuel spent with the Washington Commanders. Just like the drafting of Stribling, the return of Samuel feels like a direct attempt to remedy this problem.

Throw in the fact that coach Kyle Shanahan has historically slow-played rookie receivers, and one could make the argument that Samuel's outlook is even more favorable than Stribling's. But since Samuel isn't being hyped the same way, he can be had much later in drafts (real-time ADP: 143.4 to Stribling's 102.3).

articles.summary: NFL News: Just when the Maxx Crosby-to-Dallas Cowboys rumors appeared to be fading away into the woods, Jerry Jones’ Super Bowl-hungry team may have given NFL f.
articles.body: Just when the Maxx Crosby-to-Dallas Cowboys rumors appeared to be fading away into the woods, Jerry Jones’ Super Bowl-hungry team may have given NFL fans a fresh reason to start talking again.The Cowboys have created more than $19 million in additional salary-cap space through a series of contract restructurings, immediately reigniting speculation about whether Dallas could make a blockbuster move for Las Vegas Raiders superstar Maxx Crosby.And one massive number hangs over the entire conversation: $30 million.That is approximately what Crosby is scheduled to earn in base salary in 2026, making any potential trade a blockbuster move that would require serious financial maneuvering. Still, with the Cowboys suddenly sitting on significantly more cap flexibility, the old Crosby-to-Dallas chatter has once again found new life. This time, it might stay longer…Cowboys suddenly have money and Maxx Crosby rumors are backNo trade has been announced. No deal has been confirmed.But in the NFL gossip mill, fresh cap space plus a previously linked superstar is more than enough to get the conversation rolling again.The Dallas Cowboys reportedly now have approx. $33 million in salary-cap space following their latest round of restructurings.The team created more than $19 million in additional room by reworking the contracts of defensive tackle Kenny Clark, tight end Jake Ferguson and cornerback DaRon Bland.Clark’s $11 million roster bonus had already been converted into a signing bonus in March 2026, while his $8.8 million base salary has now reportedly been restructured as well. Bland’s $12 million base salary was converted into a signing bonus, while Ferguson’s $7.25 million base salary was also reworked.Those moves do not necessarily mean the Cowboys are preparing to trade for Crosby. However, the timing is impossible to ignore.Dallas had already been connected to the Las Vegas Raiders star edge defender earlier in the 2026 offseason, and the Cowboys’ sudden financial flexibility has undoubtedly reopened Pandora’s box.For a team with the longest-sought Super Bowl ambitions and a Year 2 head coach [Brian Schottenheimer], adding one of the NFL’s most destructive pass rushers would certainly qualify as a franchise-altering move. Other than just a news-grabbing headline.Especially when the season is just a week away. Can’t wait!The $30 million similarity standing between Dallas Cowboys and Maxx CrosbyPreviously, the Dallas Cowboys had $14 million in spending room. They created more than $19 million in additional 2026 cap space.This brings their total to more than $30 million in 2026 cap space. They have ample room to absorb a veteran [or two] via trade, according to Mike Florio of NBC Sports.According to Spotrac, Crosby signed a three-year, $106 million contract with the Raiders in 2025. The deal included $91 million guaranteed and carries an average annual value of roughly $35 million.In 2026, Crosby is scheduled to earn a $30 million base salary while carrying a $35 million cap hit. His contract also comes with a reported $64 million dead-cap figure.Anyhow, the Cowboys’ new cap space is significant, but it would not automatically make a trade financially easy. Crosby comes with a heavy dead-cap figure.Dallas would likely need additional cap maneuvering or a contract restructuring to make the numbers work. The Cowboys would also have to consider the long-term impact of adding another massive financial commitment to their roster.Why Cowboys fans refuse to let the Maxx Crosby rumors fade awayThe latest speculation did not emerge out of nowhere.Dallas had previously been mentioned among teams connected to Crosby during the Raiders star’s uncertain trade situation earlier in the 2026 offseason. That previous connection is exactly why the Cowboys’ latest cap moves have sparked another robust round of rumors.Crosby is not just another available pass rusher.He is one of the league’s elite defensive stars and the type of player who could instantly change the complexion of a defense. For a team desperately chasing a Super Bowl, the grab-worthy opportunity to add that level of proven production would be impossible to ignore.Of course, there is a massive difference between being interested in a player and actually completing a trade.The Cowboys and Raiders would need to agree on compensation, while Dallas would also need to find a way to make Crosby’s contract financially manageable.And Las Vegas would first have to decide that moving one of its biggest defensive stars is even worth considering. They did once with the Baltimore Ravens; could they do it again?Is a Maxx Crosby trade to the Dallas Cowboys literally realistic?For now, it remains speculation. There is no confirmed trade, no public sign of an agreement, and Dallas creating cap space is not proof that a deal is imminent.Still, the Cowboys have more financial flexibility, Crosby has been linked to Dallas before, and his massive salary has added fresh fuel to the speculation.The financial hurdles remain enormous, but with Jerry Jones’ appetite for blockbuster moves, the Crosby-to-Dallas rumors are officially back - and they may not be going away anytime soon…Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Pro Football Hall of Fame making massive overhaul of its selection process following 2026 Bill Belichick snub
articles.summary: The Pro Football Hall of Fame is slashing its selection committee from 50 to 28 members and eliminating the senior category in a sweeping overhaul.
articles.body: The Pro Football Hall of Fame is making massive changes to its process for picking future Hall of Famers. The Hall says it is hoping to "improve its selection process" from one that led to the 2026 class not including former New England Patriots head coach Bill Belichick as one of its "most-deserving" candidates as a first-ballot Hall of Famer. "The Hall continually reviews its bylaws to ensure the selection process reflects the highest standards of integrity and the magnitude of election to the Pro Football Hall of Fame," said Hall of Fame president Jim Porter. "There is no more important task at the Hall of Fame than the election of each new class." FOOTBALL LEGEND BILL BELICHICK ADDRESSES HALL OF FAME SNUB AND WHETHER IT WAS A 'POLITICAL' DECISION The Hall has decided to cut the number of selectors from 50 people down to 28. Of that reduced number, three will be non-voting alternates. That means the days when every NFL team had a representative intimately tied to that team on the selection committee are over. Some current selectors who are being removed will be asked to participate in various Hall of Fame committees. The identity of the selectors remaining and those removed is still being decided by the Hall of Fame, according to Porter. As some selectors are being eliminated so is the traditional system of presentation. For decades selectors presented Hall candidates to the rest of the selectors by stating a case for that person using statistics, testimony and endorsements from various respected football sources. The entire group of selectors would then debate the pros and cons of that candidate before voting. Under the new system, one voice from a non-selector will introduce each candidate by simply announcing his name and sharing his resume. Then the reduced group of selectors will go immediately into discussion on the merits of that candidate. So, why is the formal presentation disappearing? The PFHOF is trying to avoid what it calls "unintended biases" in its selection process and one way to do that is to limit the advantage some selectors have had because of their superior oratory skills over others, according to the Hall. The categories the selection committee will now consider have been cut to three: Player. Coach. Contributor. The past splitting of players into modern-era players and senior players will end. All players from all eras not currently in the Hall of Fame will all be lumped into one category for nomination. The Hall is believed to be eliminating the senior category so there is no emotional bias toward trying to select a player, say, in his final year as a modern-era candidate, before he disappears into the so-called senior category abyss. That abyss, by the way, has spit out 19 seniors being selected to the Hall in the last seven years. So this new approach is like the proverbial pendulum swinging away from a concentration on senior candidates being selected. CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM The Hall intends to have a coach and contributor subcommittee each consisting of 11 voting selectors and three alternates. Those will consist of some current selectors not chosen among the overall 28. Those committees will put forward one coach and one contributor to be considered as candidates by the greater group of selectors. A contributor, by the way, is someone who added to the game outside of playing or coaching. So broadcasters, owners, executives, commissioners and others are eligible. If contributors also played, coached, or served as an executive, their whole body of work will be considered. Every year the Hall expects to consider 13 players, one coach and one contributor as its candidates. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Hall of Fame says its class sizes will range from three to seven inductees every year. The typical number of enshrinees is more likely to be five or six because of the math involved. The reduced number of selectors will meet in person once a year, with the next meeting scheduled for the first week of Feb. 2027. FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

articles.title: “Glad Patrick was there for the kids”: Patrick Mahomes sparks emotional reactions after Chiefs star makes special Make-A-Wish visit to young fans

articles.body: Patrick Mahomes gave two young members of Chiefs Kingdom a day to remember after teaming up with Make-A-Wish and 15 and the Mahomies for a special visit. The Kansas City Chiefs shared photos of Mahomes with Tyler and Stock, two young fans who are dealing with respiratory and heart challenges, respectively, while still holding on to their love for the team.The post struck an emotional chord with Chiefs fans, who quickly filled the replies with prayers, encouragement and a few lighthearted comments about their favorite quarterback.Chiefs fans rally behind Tyler and Stock after Patrick Mahomes visitThe Chiefs shared the special moment on September 4, posting several pictures of Mahomes spending time with Tyler and Stock. In one photo, Mahomes stands between the two young fans, while another shows him signing a football for one of them. The pictures captured a relaxed moment between the quarterback and the youngsters as they got to spend time inside the Chiefs environment.The post read, “Thanks to Make-A-Wish and @15andMahomies, we welcomed Tyler and Stock today! Despite facing respiratory and heart challenges, respectively, these two are dedicated members of Chiefs Kingdom. We're rooting for you both!”The post had already picked up more than 64,000 views along with hundreds of likes and dozens of reposts when the screenshot was captured, showing how quickly the story reached the team's fanbase.The replies were filled with support for Tyler and Stock. Bernard F. Albers kept his message simple, responding with two prayer emojis, while another fan, Music2MyEars, sent a longer message wishing the youngsters well.“Sending love and prayers for good health and long happy, loving lives!! How bout those CHIEFS!!! Let's go!!”Another fan added, “Okay, glad Patrick was there for the kids, but then he went home to wrap himself in bubble wrap, right? Right?”The comment drew attention because Chiefs fans have plenty of reasons to want Mahomes protected, especially with the quarterback carrying such a huge role for the franchise. Still, the focus of the conversation remained on the two young supporters and the special opportunity they received.Another fan, Michael Lynn Walker, connected the visit to Mahomes' college background and his Texas Tech roots.“The Texas Tech guy demonstrating West Texas and Midwestern hospitality. Wreck 'em, Tech!! Wreck 'em, Chiefs!!”The different reactions showed the range of emotions surrounding the post. Some fans immediately turned to prayers, others wished Tyler and Stock good health, while others simply enjoyed seeing Mahomes take time away from football to make two young supporters feel special. Myka’s Make-A-Wish experience showed why moments like this is important Mahomes' latest visit also brings back memories of his meeting with Myka, a 12-year-old Chiefs fan from Yorba Linda who was featured in ESPN's “My Wish” series after getting the opportunity to meet her favorite quarterback.Myka had been born with a congenital heart defect and underwent two open-heart surgeries as an infant. Despite facing the possibility of additional surgeries and complications, she continued to pursue her love for football and became the quarterback of her flag football team. She even dreamed of becoming the first woman to play quarterback in the NFL.The Chiefs were Myka's favorite team, while Mahomes was the player she most wanted to meet. Make-A-Wish eventually turned that dream into a trip to Kansas City, with KC Wolf surprising Myka and her family before she traveled to meet the quarterback.Once she arrived, Myka visited the Chiefs locker room and received personalized team gear before heading onto the practice field. She met Mahomes, Travis Kelce and general manager Brett Veach, giving her the opportunity to do something that most young football fans could only imagine.Mahomes also made sure the experience felt like a football day rather than a simple meet-and-greet. He drew up a quick slant for Myka, who copied his cadence before throwing a pass to Kelce. She later launched a deep ball that Kelce caught, prompting an excited reaction from Mahomes.The quarterback then joked with her about potentially taking his job. “Don’t take my spot, though,” Mahomes said to Myka. “You can’t throw it too good.”Myka later sat down with Mahomes to break down film, including his game-winning touchdown pass to Kelce in Kansas City's divisional-round playoff win over the Buffalo Bills. She asked Mahomes what it felt like to make that play, and his answer gave her another personal look at one of the biggest moments of his career. “I was almost in shock,” Mahomes said. “I just ran to Travis and hugged him. I was just like, ‘Man, I love you. We’ll have this forever.’”The experience meant just as much to Myka's family. articles.summary: NFL News: For nearly two decades, Mike Tomlin was synonymous with the Pittsburgh Steelers. Sundays, game plans, locker rooms, and the heavy responsibility of le.
articles.body: For nearly two decades, Mike Tomlin was synonymous with the Pittsburgh Steelers. Sundays, game plans, locker rooms, and the heavy responsibility of leading one of the league’s most historic organizations defined his entire life.But stepping away from coaching in 2026 seems to have given Tomlin something he rarely had during his years on the sidelines: costly and valuable time.The former Steelers head coach has been blissfully enjoying his first extended break from the demands of coaching, and according to a clip shared by Josh Chambers on X, Tomlin opened up about how his personal time was lost in leading an NFL organization.“I’ve enjoyed 2026, man,” Tomlin said. “The free time, had an opportunity to really just focus on my wellness.”It is a revealing look at the other side of professional football - one that fans rarely get to see from a coach’s perspective, coaches who spend years living under the constant pressure of winning.Mike Tomlin’s long awaited time for himselfTomlin stepped away from the Steelers following the 2025 season, ending an impeccable 19-year run as the franchise’s head coach.He has since moved into broadcasting with NBC, joining the Football Night in America team for the 2026 season. Reportedly taking Chris Simms’ spot after Simms spoke about untouched Mike Vrabel and Dianna Russini scandal.But away from the weekly grind of preparing an NFL team, Tomlin has apparently discovered just how much of his life had been consumed by the laborious job.Coaching is often described as a year-round profession, particularly at the NFL level. Even when games are not being played, there are meetings, scouting, roster decisions, travel, and preparations for the next challenge. Apart from the constant fear of being fired after a failed season.For Tomlin, the much-needed break has offered a rare opportunity to slow down.“Man, when you lead a football team and football organization, sometimes you put yourself last. So, it’s been good to kind of focus on some things like that and really just have time to be present with my family and friends,” Tomlin said.Steelers’ coach had a stunning family reunionPerhaps the most arresting detail from Tomlin’s self-reflection was his admission that he had not attended a family reunion since 1997. When he joined Arkansas State as wide receivers coach.That shocking revelation puts into perspective how long his professional responsibilities have shaped his hectic schedule and limited his personal life.Tomlin began his coaching career in the mid-1990s and spent years climbing through college football and NFL coaching jobs before becoming the Steelers’ head coach in 2007. By the time he stepped away from Pittsburgh, football had been at the central focus of his professional life for decades.His absence from family reunions for nearly three decades highlights the costly sacrifices that can come with a coaching career.“I went to a family reunion a couple of weeks ago. I hadn’t been to a family reunion since 1997. The family reunion is always the third week in July. Where have I been all of my adult life the third week in July? In a football camp. My family was laughing that I was there,” Tomlin said.Could time away make Mike Tomlin come back to coaching?The burning question, of course, is whether this newfound freedom will ultimately make Mike Tomlin want to return to coaching - or make him appreciate life away from the sideline even more.“It’s crazy how quickly you can get used to chilling! You know what I mean? I’ve enjoyed 2026, man, the free time. Had an opportunity to really just focus on my wellness and getting into shape and things of that nature,” Tomlin said.For now, Tomlin has publicly suggested that he is enjoying his new broadcasting chapter and has not indicated that he is rushing back into an NFL coaching job. He also said that he was enjoying the new camaraderie he developed with television.After spending almost two decades carrying the expectations of an NFL franchise, Tomlin’s 2026 may be less about football and more about rediscovering everything football forced him to put on hold. Like family, for instance.And after missing family reunions since 1997, that may be the most worthwhile part of his year away from coaching.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Pro Football Hall of Fame Makes Rule Changes to Selection Process After Bill Belichick Snub
articles.summary: The Pro Football Hall of Fame is overhauling its selection process after a controversial vote left Bill Belichick out of the 2026 class.
articles.body:
The Pro Football Hall of Fame is overhauling its selection process after a controversial vote left Bill Belichick out of the 2026 class.

The Hall of Fame announced Friday that fewer people will be voting and fewer players will be inducted starting with the Class of 2027.

The changes will start with the selection committee, which will decrease from 50 to 25 voters and three non-voters.

The Athletic Completes Dianna Russini Review

Player finalists will drop from a maximum of 18 players, including up to three players who have been retired for 25 years, to 13 total players following the elimination of the separate "seniors" category.

Coaches and contributors were previously considered alongside seniors in a separate pool from modern-era players.

Voters will now consider one coach and one contributor alongside all players in a single 15-person pool of finalists.

The makeup of the selection committee, which previously included one selector from every NFL club, will also be changing.

The committee will now be made up of 27 at-large selectors and one Pro Football Writers of America representative.

The identities of the three non-voting members will rotate annually. All 28 members will meet at an in-person annual meeting, ending a six-year stretch of virtual meetings.

The new selection committee announced after the 50 previous members of the group are notified as to their future status, according to the HOF.

Hall of Fame president and CEO Jim Porter said in a statement there were "unintended biases" created by the previous voting structure, including "disparate skills of the individuals making the initial presentations of nominees for election at the annual meeting."

Initial presentations at the selection meeting will now be made by someone outside the selection committee going forward.

The Hall of Fame is also expanding who counts as a contributor, which was previously defined as someone who "made outstanding contributions to professional football in capacities other than playing or coaching."

The HOF will now allow voters to consider "a candidate's full football résumé that may include playing, coaching and other contributions to the sport" when selecting for the category.

Another notable change being made to the selection process is that candidates who make it to the final seven will not automatically be named finalists the following year.

Willie Anderson, Marshal Yanda and Terrell Suggs made it to the final seven of the 2026 voting process but will no longer be automatic finalists for 2027.

The retirement periods before eligibility remain one season for coaches and five for players, with no minimum requirement for contributors.

The 2026 Pro Football Hall of Fame class featured five players, the smallest group since 2025. First-timers eligible for the 2027 class include Ben Roethlisberger, Rob Gronkowski and Adrian Peterson.

articles.title: Kirk Herbstreit’s college football warning raises tough questions as ESPN’s College GameDay veteran enters 30th season
articles.summary: NFL News: Kirk Herbstreit is entering his 30th season with ESPN’s College GameDay, but the veteran commentator is not happy with the direction college football .
articles.body: Kirk Herbstreit is entering his 30th season with ESPN’s College GameDay, but the veteran commentator is not happy with the direction college football has taken. In a new interview with PEOPLE, the former Ohio State quarterback spoke about the major changes he has seen during his three decades on the show. Herbstreit said the sport has changed more in the last three or four years than it did in the previous 100, and he believes a lack of clear leadership has made things harder to follow.Kirk Herbstreit points to major changes in college footballHerbstreit joined ESPN in 1995 and tried out for College GameDay a year later. He was only 26 when he got the role, even though he did not expect to get it. Looking back, he told PEOPLE, “I stumbled into getting this opportunity at ESPN.”Three decades later, Herbstreit has watched college football change in ways he never expected. The growth of the transfer portal, player rights, government involvement and court decisions has created a very different sport from the one he knew when he started.“I mean, really in the last three or four years, I think we’ve seen more change than the previous hundred years—and not always for the better,” Herbstreit said. “It’s been frustrating at times to watch.”One of his biggest concerns is the lack of a clear authority that can set and enforce rules across the sport. He also questioned how much power players now have compared with the past.“We have these district judges all over the country making unbelievable rulings that make no sense, and there’s no one there to stop them,” Herbstreit said. “The players went from having absolutely no say to now all the say. And that doesn’t make any sense to me either.”Kirk Herbstreit remains hopeful about College GameDay and college footballDespite his concerns, Herbstreit does not believe college football has lost what makes it special. He pointed to the atmosphere around games as proof that fans still care deeply about the sport.“You go out to these games and the stadiums are full, the marching bands come out, the student sections are full,” he said. “Here come the teams and their uniforms, and it’s still an incredible celebration on Saturday.”That popularity gives Herbstreit some hope that the sport can eventually find a clearer path. He believes the current problems need to be addressed, but he still sees plenty worth celebrating on Saturdays.“The ratings have never been higher. The interest in the sport has never been bigger,” Herbstreit said. “I’m hopeful that we get some direction here in the next year or two to try to make some sense of where we are.”Herbstreit will now begin another season on College GameDay as the show returns Saturday, Sept. 5, from Baton Rouge, Louisiana.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: New Fantasy Football 2026 Printable Cheat Sheet and PPR Mock Draft Strategy
articles.summary: With opening kick of the 2026 NFL season just around the corner, your pre-draft toolkit for fantasy football should be fully loaded.
articles.body:
With opening kick of the 2026 NFL season just around the corner, your pre-draft toolkit for fantasy football should be fully loaded.

While all of the elements have their place, the most valuable resource in that toolbox is a mock draft.

Nothing gets you better prepared for the real thing. You're feeling the same pressure of drafting against managers (human or simulated) while also keeping an eye out for any notable trends that may well wind up tweaking your actual draft approach.

So, as you finish out the remainder of mock draft season, we're here to discuss a couple of mock strategies to employ after providing cheat sheet-style positional rankings.

The PPR format might point some toward wide receivers and top-shelf tight ends, but the running back position looms largest as a fantasy gold mine.

There's just a different kind of safety with a running back who will handle, say, 20-ish touches per game than there is with a receiver who sees 10 or so targets. Not to mention, the running back ranks thin out a lot sooner than wide receiver does.

So, as long as the draft board allows it, you should plan on hammering the running back spot early and often. If you can snag two with your first three picks, do it. If you can find three or even four intriguing options with your first eight selections, do that, too.

You'll want a difference-maker or two at the top, but you'll also want some reliable depth pieces (ideally capable of filling a flex spot right away) given the inherent injury risks at the position. If your running back room is among the strongest in the league, the chances are the same applies to your roster as a whole.

This strategy has been repeated so often it almost feels cliched to say. But there's a reason behind the repetition: The advice is sound (and advisable!).

As awesome as someone like Josh Allen is, there is a massive opportunity cost that comes with spending the second- or third-round pick so often needed to land him. You'll be hurting at a premium position by doing so, and you might need to strike gold on a couple of lottery-ticket sleepers to compensate.

There just isn't the same give-and-take with waiting on a quarterback. If your league starts one signal-caller (as most do), there are more than enough to go around to give everyone a rock-solid option. You could be one of the last managers in your draft to take a quarterback and still walk away with the likes of Matthew Stafford, Brock Purdy or Jared Goff.

If you waited that long to take a starting running back or receiver, your roster might be toast. At quarterback, though, you can basically wait as long as possible and still snag someone who might throw for 4,000-plus yards and 30-plus touchdowns.
